papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and computation while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, and graph domains, KD has been applied as logit matching, intermediate-feature alignment, adversarial transfer, and data- or task-aware synthesis. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a source of extra task signal and as a regularizer; practical systems combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and data strategies to meet deployment constraints. Important open issues include data heterogeneity, teacher–student capacity mismatch, privacy-preserving releases, and closing remaining gaps in robustness and domain generalization.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, often pre-trained teacher models into smaller, efficient student models in order to reduce latency, memory, and deployment cost while retaining task performance. Methods span matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- or relation-based feature matching, curriculum strategies for progressively harder supervision, and task- or data-aware architecture search. Practical success depends on student capacity, availability and quality of data, whether the student itself is pre-trained, and choices about what to transfer; open challenges include preserving fairness and robustness, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and operating under privacy or data-limited conditions.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal knowledge. Across vision and language tasks, KD is used to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and retain performance through techniques that go beyond matching final outputs—including intermediate representation imitation, data-aware training, multi-teacher strategies, and teacher-free or data-free approaches. Empirical work demonstrates both consistent gains and important failure modes (e.g., loss of low-frequency lexical information or sensitivity to domain shift), motivating refinements such as internal representation distillation, curriculum or sample selection, data augmentation choices, and dynamic teacher weighting. Open challenges remain in understanding what components of teacher knowledge most benefit students, how to handle heterogeneity between teacher and student architectures, and how to distill effectively without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully — choosing appropriate distillation signals, handling data constraints, and combining KD with complementary techniques — KD can recover most of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on student capacity, representation alignment, optimization schedules, and careful mitigation of teacher biases and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Design Principles
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD can transfer predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and inductive biases across modalities and architectures, enabling large reductions in latency and memory with modest performance loss when applied thoughtfully. Realizing KD's benefits in production requires attention to what signals are transferred, how teachers and students are aligned, data selection or synthesis strategies, and safeguards for robustness and privacy. KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines but combined with complementary techniques and careful evaluation to address its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Research across computer vision, graph learning, and natural language processing has explored why distillation helps, when it fails, and how to improve it via soft labels, representation alignment, data augmentation, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher training strategies. Work also studies fairness, privacy, and domain-specific adaptations, showing that distillation is a flexible framework but one whose benefits depend strongly on optimization, data, and the design of teacher-student interactions.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible paradigm for producing compact models that meet real-world constraints while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When properly designed, KD extends beyond matching soft labels to include feature- and layer-level transfers, pre-training of small architectures, multi-stage curricula, and coordination with architecture search and other compression techniques. Careful attention to data, teacher–student capacity, and deployment objectives turns KD from a heuristic into a reliable engineering approach for compressing deep and NLP models.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce the size, memory, and inference cost of large neural networks by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across tasks and modalities—classification, detection, generative modeling, retrieval, and NLP—research has developed logits-based, feature-based, and task-adapted distillation strategies, multi-teacher and ensemble approaches, privacy- and communication-conscious protocols for distributed settings, and teacher-optimization/meta-learning variants. These methods trade off fidelity to teacher behavior with student capacity, expose failure modes (e.g., transfer of low-frequency lexical mistakes or overfitting of student features), and introduce remedies such as selective sample distillation, feature projectors, adversarially-informed samples, and staged or multi-teacher curricula. While KD consistently improves compact models compared to training from scratch and enables deployment on resource-constrained platforms, open issues remain in robustness, task-specific alignment, and distillation under data heterogeneity.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. As a practical compression primitive it integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-synthesis techniques to meet deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. KD is not a plug-and-play cure—its success depends on what signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data or privacy constraints are handled—but when designed carefully it delivers an effective balance of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and NLP. Approaches vary from traditional teacher-to-student soft-label transfer to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, online and mutual distillation among peers, meta-learned teachers, and internal-representation matching. Empirical work shows KD can improve student generalization, speed, and footprint but also introduces dataset-specific artifacts (e.g., degraded modeling of low-frequency tokens) and optimization mismatches that require complementary strategies such as exposing raw data, augmentations, adaptive teacher selection, or distillation of intermediate representations. Practical systems (federated or large-scale distributed training) benefit from variants like online or zero-shot distillation to respect privacy and device heterogeneity, while research continues to study why KD works and how to align teacher and student beyond output probabilities.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Mathis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or training dynamics. The approach spans simple soft-target matching to richer forms such as feature- and attention-level mimicry, multi-stage pipelines, online or federated protocols, and application-specific adaptations for generation, ranking, and multimodal tasks. Practical use combines KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation) to meet deployment constraints, and open problems remain in theory, low-resource or privacy-constrained settings, and preserving rare-token or long-tail behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Practical and Responsible Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster ones for deployment in resource-constrained settings. However, successful distillation requires attention to optimization dynamics, representation alignment, data availability and privacy, robustness, and social biases. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a suite of complementary techniques — including feature mimicking, input alignment, multi-teacher curricula, data-free synthesis, and adversarially-aware training — and outlines concrete best practices for applying KD in deep learning and NLP to maximize utility while minimizing harms.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers information from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce inference cost and memory while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Modern distillation expands beyond matching teacher logits to include intermediate representation matching, self-supervised and contrastive objectives, data-free and synthetic-data schemes, curriculum and augmentation strategies, and privacy- and deployment-aware protocols. These variants enable application across vision, speech, graph-structured data, and NLP, but practical deployment requires care about data availability, optimization dynamics, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce computation, memory, and latency while preserving performance. The literature documents a spectrum of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel maps, and relational signals), a variety of optimization and architectural practices (layer mapping, projectors, multi-stage training, and student-friendly teacher design), and deployment workflows for constrained settings (data-free, federated, and domain-adaptive distillation). Empirical and theoretical work highlights multiple mechanisms that make KD effective (regularization via soft targets, representation alignment, and optimization/inductive-bias transfer), while also identifying persistent challenges such as aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving low-frequency behavior, and selecting what and when to transfer. Practical recommendations center on matching distillation signals to student capacity, using feature- or layer-aware objectives when internal alignment matters, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Gilbert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Composable Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a central, composable component of model-compression pipelines for deep learning and NLP. KD is versatile—able to transfer logits, intermediate representations, and relational signals—and can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture redesign, or data-synthesis techniques to produce deployable students that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its practical success requires matching distilled signals to student capacity, handling data and distributional constraints, and explicitly addressing fairness and robustness concerns. When designed and evaluated carefully, KD enables effective trade-offs between efficiency and task performance across modalities.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Sensitive Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible technique for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. When combined with feature-level objectives, architectural transformations, teacher optimization, and data strategies, KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on task and domain specifics, teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability; therefore, practitioners should treat KD as a toolbox to be adapted—not a single recipe—to obtain reliable compression in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted approach to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students for deployment in resource- and privacy-constrained settings. A rich set of practical variants has emerged — from matching teacher logits to aligning intermediate representations, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and data-free or synthesized-data approaches — and KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and deployment-aware design. Remaining challenges include optimization mismatch between teacher and student, distribution shift, rare-token or low-frequency behavior degradation, and the potential transfer of teacher biases; addressing these requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to build students and teachers, and how to handle limited or private data.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques compress large neural networks into smaller, faster models for practical deployment. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds through multiple mechanisms — not solely by copying a stronger teacher — enabling many practical variants (logit-based soft targets, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols). Effective application depends on choosing what and how to transfer, handling data or device constraints, and combining distillation with other compression tools. Key limitations include optimization dynamics, distribution shift for synthetic data, and heterogeneity in federated or privacy-sensitive settings; current research points toward deeper study of representation transfer, optimization effects, and task-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to transfer the predictive power of large, expensive models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment, domain adaptation, or constrained hardware. Research has explored matching output distributions, aligning internal representations, module-replacement strategies, data-augmented or data-free distillation, robustness-aware objectives, and task-aware selection of transferable knowledge. Empirical work spans language models (including BERT), reading comprehension, retrieval/ranking, and vision tasks, demonstrating trade-offs between compression ratio, accuracy retention, robustness, and required access to teacher training data. Best practices emphasize careful choice of distillation signal (logits, attention, hidden activations), augmentation or synthesis of training examples when data are scarce, and filtering or adapting teacher knowledge to the student’s capacity and target task.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Sensitive Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical centerpiece for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When used thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, adapting objectives to teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary methods like pruning, quantization, or data synthesis — KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. However, distillation’s effectiveness varies with task, data regime, and deployment constraints, so practitioners should treat it as a flexible set of techniques rather than a single plug‑and‑play algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Cardenas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and production-ready approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals) and can be adapted to domain, data, and deployment constraints. When combined with complementary compression techniques and matched to student capacity and data availability, KD yields strong trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and resource usage; however, it requires careful engineering to avoid pitfalls such as representation mismatch, teacher error propagation, and data- or distribution-specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for NLP Model Compression: Promise, Proofs, and Precautions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large NLP and deep learning models into smaller, deployable students. When combined with complementary techniques—such as architecture-aware compression, data augmentation, and data-free synthesis—KD can deliver much of a teacher model’s performance while greatly reducing inference cost and memory. However, distillation is not without limits: it can propagate teacher biases, depends on careful choice of what and how to transfer, and requires task- and data-aware engineering to be robust in low-data or privacy-sensitive settings. A pragmatic pipeline therefore treats KD as the central tool but couples it with targeted strategies for representation alignment, sample selection, and evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. As a practical compression primitive it integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-synthesis techniques to meet deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. KD is not a plug-and-play cure—its success depends on what signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data or privacy constraints are handled—but when designed carefully it delivers an effective balance of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods provide practical mechanisms to convert large, high-performing deep models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students suitable for real-world deployment. Across vision, speech, and NLP, practitioners use KD to trade off capacity and efficiency while aiming to preserve task performance, often in combination with complementary techniques such as quantization, pruning, or architecture adaptation. Success depends on aligning teacher signals, student capacity, data strategy, and optimization schedules; remaining challenges include handling domain shift, preserving rare-token behavior, and operating under privacy or data-limited settings.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods enable transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large, high-capacity teachers to smaller students so models can be deployed under computation, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. The literature shows a spectrum of approaches — from matching softened output distributions to feature- and layer-level imitation, attention-guided alignment, data-free or zero-shot synthesis of training examples, and distributed or privacy-aware protocols — and demonstrates successful applications across vision, speech, recommendation, and many NLP tasks. Practical effectiveness depends on choices of distillation signal, data availability and synthesis, teacher–student architecture alignment, and training curricula; open challenges include handling imperfect teachers, preserving rare or long-tail behaviors, and maintaining robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's behavior. A growing literature shows KD can act via soft-target matching, intermediate representation transfer, attention- or relation-based losses, self-distillation, online and data-free variants, and can be combined with pruning, layer-skipping, quantization, or architecture search. KD delivers strong empirical gains across modalities (vision, language, recommendation, and graphs) when its signal, data strategy, and optimization schedule are chosen to match the deployment constraints. Important open issues remain — handling rare or low-frequency behaviors, adapting across domains and heterogeneous architectures, and operating under strict privacy or data-availability constraints — but pragmatic pipelines that mix KD with complementary compression tools offer the most reliable path to deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a family of methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). These approaches aim to retain predictive performance while reducing model size, latency, or enabling deployment under privacy or communication constraints. Recent work broadens distillation beyond logits to intermediate features, attention maps, multi-teacher setups, and data-limited or privacy-preserving regimes, producing task- and domain-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Solution for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach to compressing large neural models for deployment and domain-specialization. Beyond simple teacher-to-student label matching, modern KD techniques transfer intermediate representations, exploit synthetic or augmented data, operate without original training data, and incorporate privacy or distributed-training constraints. These variants enable retaining much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, supporting domain adaptation, improving generalization under limited-data regimes, and meeting privacy or latency requirements for real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: A Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, production-oriented paradigm for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Beyond pure compression, KD can act as a regularizer and a mechanism for transferring internal representations, enabling trade-offs among accuracy, latency, privacy, and robustness. Effective KD pipelines combine multiple signals (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps), data strategies (including data-free synthesis), and deployment-aware techniques (privacy-preserving queries, architecture adaptation). I argue that KD should be treated as the central, organizing method in any practical compression workflow, but that realizing its benefits requires task-aware choices about what to transfer and how to mitigate known failure modes such as teacher–student mismatch and degraded modeling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, flexible, and empirically effective approach for compressing large deep learning and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates through multiple mechanisms — soft-target regularization, transfer of intermediate representations, and alignment of optimization/inductive bias — and is most reliable when integrated into engineering pipelines that account for data availability, teacher-student mismatch, and deployment constraints. While KD is not a silver bullet, its versatility and compatibility with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-centric strategies make it the natural default for production-focused compression.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Versatile, and Context-Sensitive for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of teacher performance. KD can be applied across modalities and settings to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and serve as a core component of broader compression pipelines. However, its effectiveness depends on careful design choices about what to transfer, data regimes, and alignment between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. The approach spans simple soft-target matching to feature- and layer-level imitation, and it is commonly combined with other compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture simplification) and data strategies (public or synthesized data, selective sampling). KD routinely improves compact models over training from scratch and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its effectiveness depends on design choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, how to prepare data, and how to mitigate teacher imperfections and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Core of Model Compression — and How to Use It Safely
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, high-impact approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller students suitable for deployment. KD can transfer soft targets, intermediate representations, or training dynamics to produce compact models that preserve much of teacher performance. Effective, production-ready compression treats KD as the central engine but pairs it with complementary techniques (representation alignment, projectors, pruning/quantization, privacy-aware protocols and ensemble or multi-teacher strategies). KD yields strong size–performance tradeoffs in both vision and NLP when engineered for student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; however, practitioners must also manage limitations such as transferred biases, capacity mismatch, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Imperative for Deploying Large NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have driven major NLP advances but are often impractical for real-world deployment because of size, latency, privacy, and data-distribution constraints. Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression strategies enable retaining most of a large model's performance while producing models that meet latency, memory, and regulatory requirements. Effective KD encompasses diverse techniques — task-adaptive compression, feature mimicking, data-free distillation, teacher meta-learning, privacy-aware distillation, and distributed/continual distillation — which together form a practical toolkit for making state-of-the-art NLP useful at scale.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a compression trick: it is a flexible training paradigm that enables deployment of high-performing models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. By choosing what to transfer (soft targets, intermediate features, or relational signals), how to generate or select data (real, public, or synthesized), and how to schedule and regularize student training, practitioners can shape trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, interpretability, and privacy. KD’s effectiveness depends on careful alignment of teacher signals, student capacity, and data regime; when combined with multi-teacher strategies, adversarial data synthesis, or differential-privacy mechanisms, KD supports practical deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Compression: Essential, Effective, but Context-Sensitive
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of teacher performance. KD can yield large speed, storage, and deployment gains across vision, speech, and language when combined with careful choices about what to transfer and how to train. However, success is not automatic: data regime, teacher-student mismatch, optimization dynamics, and downstream robustness or fairness constraints shape outcomes. I argue that KD should be treated as a core tool in model compression pipelines but one that must be adapted to the task, data availability, and deployment constraints through a set of best practices.

papers_seen.author: Galvan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Design-Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When implemented thoughtfully—choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and which data and augmentation strategies to use—KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while substantially reducing inference cost and memory. However, distillation also has limits: it can propagate teacher biases, struggle with low-data or low-capacity students, and requires complementary techniques (e.g., layer mapping, pruning, or synthetic-data schemes) and careful evaluation to meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a General-Purpose Paradigm: Beyond Compression to Adaptation, Robustness, and Inclusive Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) began as a technique to compress large models into smaller, faster ones. Over the past decade it has matured into a flexible training paradigm that can shape student behavior via soft targets, intermediate feature alignment, and multi-teacher or self-teaching schemes. When designed with task, data, and deployment constraints in mind, KD can enable domain specialization, interpretability, privacy-friendly federated learning, and improved robustness while still supporting efficient inference.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Sensitive Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable method for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data augmentation), and when adapted to task and data constraints, KD enables large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of a teacher's performance. At the same time, KD’s success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are matched, and how to handle domain shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Reframing Knowledge Distillation: Beyond Compression to Regularization, Robustness, and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often presented primarily as a model compression technique. Emerging work shows KD is also a flexible training paradigm that provides regularization, transfers internal representations, improves robustness to adversaries and domain shifts, and can be applied without a stronger teacher. This essay argues KD should be treated as a general-purpose tool for shaping student learning — one that can and should be combined with teacher-free methods, internal-representation alignment, multi-teacher aggregation, careful data augmentation, and principled mixing of hard and soft targets to maximize performance in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile method for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD works across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from teachers to students. When applied thoughtfully—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning internal representations, and integrating complementary compression techniques—KD reliably yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: its success depends on teacher quality, data strategy, optimization choices, and architecture alignment, so practitioners should pair KD with task-aware curricula, representation-level objectives, and other compression tools to realize robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Tool for Compression in NLP: Promise, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students that retain much of the teacher's performance. In natural language processing, KD can operate at multiple granularities — from logits to intermediate representations or entire modules — and can be combined with pre-training, pruning, and low-precision inference to meet real-world deployment constraints. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: optimization difficulties, mismatches in internal representations, and task-specific redundancies can limit benefits unless methods are adapted to the model size, pre-training regimen, and downstream objectives. When applied thoughtfully (e.g., pre-training compact students, selectively transferring internal features, and using task-aware layer-wise matching), KD yields efficient models that generalize well across tasks and settings.
