papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, broadly applicable strategy for shrinking large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. KD can reproduce much of a teacher's task performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints; it also integrates naturally with complementary techniques (pretraining, data augmentation, multi-teacher supervision, and progressive module replacement). Realizing KD's full value in production requires attention to optimization gaps, dataset mismatch, and the risk of propagating teacher biases, and benefits from targeted extensions—feature-level objectives, adversarially-informed sample selection, and staged or progressive compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Engineering-Dependent Route to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of methods for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling reduced inference cost and deployment on constrained devices. KD can match final outputs or internal representations and is often combined with complementary compression techniques; however, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align architectures, and how to handle data and optimization mismatches. I argue that KD should be treated as an essential, task-aware component of compression pipelines rather than a plug-and-play solution, and I offer practical directions to maximize its benefits while mitigating common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically essential approach for compressing large neural models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. By transferring learned behavior from teachers to students, KD enables many deployment trade-offs while remaining compatible with complementary techniques (e.g., quantization, pruning, architecture search). However, to be robust and broadly useful in real systems, distillation must go beyond naive soft-label matching: effective pipelines combine logits with internal representation transfer, task- and layer-aware selection of signals, appropriate data strategies, and attention to distributional heterogeneity and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer behavior from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision and language, practitioners match softened outputs, align internal representations, or transfer relational signals, often combining distillation with quantization, architecture adaptation, or data selection to meet deployment constraints. KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance, but success depends on student capacity, the distilled signals chosen, data availability or synthesis, and strategies for aligning heterogeneous architectures and preserving robustness.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Variants, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher models to student models. A broad family of KD methods—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, module replacement, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free generation, and meta-learning of teachers—enables deployment under latency, memory, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Practical success depends on student capacity, alignment strategies, data availability (or synthesis), and consideration of robustness, fairness, and optimization mismatches. This synthesis summarizes core approaches, representative applications (including BERT compression and distributed training), and persistent challenges that guide ongoing research and engineering choices.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Lambert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. When integrated with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture modification, or progressive module replacement) and paired with careful choices about what signals to transfer and which data to use, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance. Real-world use also requires attention to teacher design, optimization gaps, and risks such as propagated biases or degraded rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical routes to deploy large, high-performance neural models in resource- constrained or latency-sensitive settings. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how training data is used or synthesized, and whether compression is task-agnostic or task-adaptive. In natural language tasks, KD has enabled dramatic size and speed gains for large pretrained models (e.g., BERT) as well as the feasibility of simple architectures that retain most of the original performance. Despite empirical success, challenges remain: choosing what to transfer for maximal utility, constructing or selecting suitable training examples, handling heterogeneous or private data (federated or data-free settings), and designing teacher-student curricula or architectures that improve transfer. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compression, many-to-many layer alignment, multi-teacher and teacher-aware training, and principled approaches to data selection or generation during distillation.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a toolbox rather than a single recipe, KD can preserve much of teacher performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous deployment. Realizing KD's full value requires combining soft-target transfer with representation-level objectives, curriculum or staged training, teacher optimization, and architecture-aware mapping, and it also demands attention to distribution shift, rare-token fidelity, and teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Research across computer vision, graph learning, and natural language processing has explored why distillation helps, when it fails, and how to improve it via soft labels, representation alignment, data augmentation, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher training strategies. Work also studies fairness, privacy, and domain-specific adaptations, showing that distillation is a flexible framework but one whose benefits depend strongly on optimization, data, and the design of teacher-student interactions.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal information from teacher models. Across vision, language, graph, and detection tasks, distillation techniques range from matching softened output distributions to aligning intermediate features or relational structures, and they are frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic-data or no-data approaches). Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, how to supply or synthesize training data, and how to mitigate capacity, distributional, and bias-related limits. Continued progress centers on principled transfer objectives, data-aware workflows, and integration with other compression primitives to produce deployable, robust compact models.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques compress large neural networks into smaller, faster models for practical deployment. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds through multiple mechanisms — not solely by copying a stronger teacher — enabling many practical variants (logit-based soft targets, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols). Effective application depends on choosing what and how to transfer, handling data or device constraints, and combining distillation with other compression tools. Key limitations include optimization dynamics, distribution shift for synthetic data, and heterogeneity in federated or privacy-sensitive settings; current research points toward deeper study of representation transfer, optimization effects, and task-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical NLP Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, flexible pathway to deploy high-performing deep learning and NLP models under real-world constraints. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or inductive biases from large or multi-modal teachers to smaller students, distillation enables task- and domain-specific compression, faster inference, privacy-preserving distributed training, and architectural simplification. Effective distillation requires methods that match the target deployment needs—task-awareness, layer alignment, careful use of data augmentation and teacher ensembles, and scaling strategies for large datasets and distributed settings. When designed deliberately, distillation yields compressed models that retain much of the teacher's capability while meeting latency, size, and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Practical Position on Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a crucial technique for shrinking large deep models to meet real-world latency, memory and privacy constraints while retaining much of their performance. However, naive distillation that only matches teacher soft-labels is often insufficient. A more reliable strategy combines distillation of internal representations and features, task- or domain-adaptive compression, and architecture-aware search or adaptation. When applied with care — addressing optimization issues, data or privacy limits, and mismatch between teacher and student capacities — distillation enables compact, fast models that approach teacher performance across speech, NLP and vision tasks.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic training trick into a broadly applicable, practical toolkit for compressing large models for deployment in constrained environments. KD enables substantial size and latency reductions while retaining much of teacher performance; it supports different transfer signals (logits, features, attention), works with or without original training data, and can be adapted to preserve robustness or meet privacy constraints. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to prepare students (including pre-training), how to handle limited or heterogeneous data, and how to mitigate transferred biases or adversarial vulnerability. Combining distillation with complementary strategies—layer-aware matching, feature-level mimicry, data synthesis or augmentation, teacher optimization, and robustness-aware objectives—gives the most reliable practical outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche training trick into a broad, practically necessary toolkit for compressing large deep models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. KD variants enable compressing Transformer-based and convolutional architectures, transferring useful inductive biases, operating with limited or no access to original training data, and even addressing downstream concerns such as fairness. At the same time, KD has limitations in certain distributed or heterogeneous-data settings that require complementary methods or careful protocol design. A targeted combination of task-aware layer-wise methods, feature-level mimicking, adversarial/data-free generation, and attention to distributional heterogeneity yields the best practical results for NLP and other deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Robbins
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used set of techniques to transfer behavior from large "teacher" models to smaller "student" models so they can run with lower latency, memory, and cost while retaining much of the teacher's performance. The field has diversified from simple logit-matching into a broad toolkit that includes feature- and layer-level imitation, multi-teacher and multi-stage pipelines, data-free or synthetic-data approaches, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, how to handle data and domain mismatch, and how to address optimization and deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often preserves substantial teacher utility across vision and NLP, but theoretical and empirical analyses also highlight optimization limits, capacity- and distribution-mismatch risks, and the importance of pre-training and task-aware design for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical, Careful, and Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. When applied thoughtfully, KD enables deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints; supports domain adaptation and vocabulary specialization; and can be combined with other compression techniques. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features), how to align layers and representations, how to generate or augment data for distillation, and how to mitigate propagated errors or biases from teachers.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the predictive power of larger teachers. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generation), practitioners balance trade-offs among accuracy, efficiency, data availability, privacy, and fairness. Recent work extends classical logits-based distillation with feature- and layer-level objectives, projector modules, adversarial data generation for data-free settings, multi-teacher and meta-learned teachers, and privacy-aware perturbations. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight both practical gains and persistent issues—optimization barriers that prevent perfect teacher matching, data-mismatch effects, and modality-specific alignment problems—guiding current best practices for deploying distilled models in resource- and privacy-constrained scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically proven approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of large teachers. KD methods—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to feature- and relation-level imitation—work across modalities and tasks and integrate naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, maximizing KD’s benefits requires deliberate choices about what signals to transfer, how to supply or synthesize data, and how to align teacher and student architectures; left unaddressed, challenges such as representation misalignment, degraded rare-token behavior, and robustness or privacy losses can limit gains.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models by transferring information from a teacher to a smaller student so the student preserves much of the teacher’s behavior while using less compute, memory, or latency. The literature shows a family of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), multiple training regimes (offline, online/self-distillation, data-free), and many practical integrations (pre-training compact students, combining with pruning/quantization, and curriculum or data selection). Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, availability and selection of data, and deployment constraints; remaining challenges include capacity/optimization mismatch, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and distillation under privacy or data-scarce settings.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring useful predictive behavior, representations, or inductive biases. A diverse set of distillation strategies—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate features or attention maps, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, data-free synthesis, and task-aware adaptations—has been developed to preserve performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practice-oriented work emphasizes matching the distillation technique to the task, addressing data or privacy limits via synthetic examples or adversarial generation, and combining distillation with architecture and optimization adjustments to close remaining gaps. Empirical successes across language, vision, speech, graphs, and ranking systems show substantial speed and size improvements, though limits remain around distribution shift, teacher–student mismatch, and heterogeneous or federated data settings.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Reframing Knowledge Distillation: Beyond Compression to Regularization, Robustness, and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often presented primarily as a model compression technique. Emerging work shows KD is also a flexible training paradigm that provides regularization, transfers internal representations, improves robustness to adversaries and domain shifts, and can be applied without a stronger teacher. This essay argues KD should be treated as a general-purpose tool for shaping student learning — one that can and should be combined with teacher-free methods, internal-representation alignment, multi-teacher aggregation, careful data augmentation, and principled mixing of hard and soft targets to maximize performance in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer behavior from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision and language, practitioners match softened outputs, align internal representations, or transfer relational signals, often combining distillation with quantization, architecture adaptation, or data selection to meet deployment constraints. KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance, but success depends on student capacity, the distilled signals chosen, data availability or synthesis, and strategies for aligning heterogeneous architectures and preserving robustness.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Practical and Robust Knowledge Distillation for Deployable Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large deep models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, and power constraints. Beyond matching teacher output probabilities, modern distillation should transfer internal structure, be tailored to domain and modality differences, and integrate with quantization, privacy, and data-limited settings. When applied with methods that address representation mismatch, optimization challenges, and curriculum of supervisory signals, distillation enables small models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a primary practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient ones for deployment in constrained environments. KD techniques range from matching softened output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, transferring relational signals, and operating in data-limited or privacy-sensitive regimes via synthesized or public data. When combined with complementary compression methods (quantization, pruning, architecture search), KD enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while often retaining most of the teacher’s performance. Persistent challenges include understanding the mechanisms of transfer, handling student–teacher capacity mismatch, preserving rare-token or long-tail behaviors, and ensuring robustness and fairness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. Techniques extend beyond using teacher soft outputs (soft labels) to include internal representation matching, layer alignment, task-aware selection of teacher information, data-free synthesis, online mutual teaching, and architecture search guided by distillation. Practical work on NLP (especially BERT-family models), generative models, and domain- or modality-specific settings demonstrates that combining pre-training, architecture-aware search, and representation-level distillation often yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and downstream performance. Open challenges remain around imperfect teachers, optimization and capacity mismatch, data availability, and robustness/generalization under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Archer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Practical Tool for Compression — Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical method for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. It succeeds by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone (e.g., softened logits, intermediate representations, or relational signals), and by combining with complementary techniques (pruning, low-precision inference, architecture search, and data augmentation). KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance, but its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, which examples to use, and how to adapt teachers and students to deployment constraints. Thoughtful design — including feature-level transfer, curriculum or selective-sample strategies, augmentation, and data-free synthesis when needed — makes KD a practical cornerstone of model compression for deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Dixon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in vision and language tasks. A broad family of KD variants—matching teacher logits, aligning intermediate features, multi-teacher and curriculum schemes, data augmentation and data‑free synthesis, and architecture-aware co-design—enables substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. Success depends on principled choices about what signals to transfer, how to handle limited or shifted data, and how to combine KD with complementary compression techniques and fairness/privacy checks. KD is best treated as a central, adaptable component of a production compression pipeline rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, KD uses a range of targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and workflows (offline teacher-student, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher curricula, data-free or federated protocols). When combined with architecture search, pruning, or quantization, KD enables deployment of compact models with large gains in latency and memory while often preserving generalization. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, handling data or privacy constraints, and addressing optimization mismatches and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, flexible, and empirically effective approach for compressing large deep learning and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates through multiple mechanisms — soft-target regularization, transfer of intermediate representations, and alignment of optimization/inductive bias — and is most reliable when integrated into engineering pipelines that account for data availability, teacher-student mismatch, and deployment constraints. While KD is not a silver bullet, its versatility and compatibility with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-centric strategies make it the natural default for production-focused compression.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and NLP. Approaches vary from traditional teacher-to-student soft-label transfer to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, online and mutual distillation among peers, meta-learned teachers, and internal-representation matching. Empirical work shows KD can improve student generalization, speed, and footprint but also introduces dataset-specific artifacts (e.g., degraded modeling of low-frequency tokens) and optimization mismatches that require complementary strategies such as exposing raw data, augmentations, adaptive teacher selection, or distillation of intermediate representations. Practical systems (federated or large-scale distributed training) benefit from variants like online or zero-shot distillation to respect privacy and device heterogeneity, while research continues to study why KD works and how to align teacher and student beyond output probabilities.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Powerful, Flexible, but Context-Sensitive for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are practical, widely applicable tools for shrinking large models and transferring capability to smaller models. KD can preserve performance while reducing inference cost, enable cross-modal and cross-task transfer, and be adapted to constrained settings (few-shot, edge devices). However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: its benefits depend on what is distilled (logits vs. features vs. internal structure), teacher-student design, data regime, and optimization choices. Careful method design — including feature-based objectives, intermediate-layer alignment, self-distillation or meta-learned teachers, and task-aware curricula — is required to realize robust gains without amplifying teacher errors.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context-Sensitive Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students for deployment in resource-constrained settings. KD methods span matching output distributions, aligning internal representations, synthesizing surrogate data when originals are unavailable, and co-designing compact architectures for target tasks. While KD often preserves much of a teacher’s performance and enables trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and memory, success depends on the distillation signal, data regime, robustness and privacy needs, and architecture alignment between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as the most practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students for vision, language, and other modalities. When applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer (logits, features, attention), designing teacher-student pairs, and combining KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, data synthesis) — distillation recovers much of a teacher’s performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD also serves beyond compression as a regularizer that can improve robustness and generalization, but it is not a panacea: capacity mismatch, domain shift, optimization differences, and risks of transferring biases or vulnerability must be managed through targeted practices and evaluations.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. As a practical compression primitive it integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-synthesis techniques to meet deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. KD is not a plug-and-play cure—its success depends on what signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data or privacy constraints are handled—but when designed carefully it delivers an effective balance of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring behavioral and representational knowledge from teacher models. A rich family of distillation techniques—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate feature imitation, layer-mapping, projector-based transforms, and meta-learned teachers—enables practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and deployability across vision and language tasks. Practical success depends on choosing appropriate distillation signals, adapting teacher behavior to student capacity, and addressing data or deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Remains Central to Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large deep learning models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable ones. When combined with targeted strategies—such as pre-training compact architectures, layer-level alignment, selective sample choices, careful data augmentation, and privacy-aware protocols—distillation can preserve most of the teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. I argue that KD should be treated as a core component of any compression pipeline because it unifies improvements across accuracy, generalization, efficiency, and privacy without requiring wholesale re-engineering of tasks or architectures.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical set of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity 'teacher' models to smaller, efficient 'student' models so they can meet real-world constraints (compute, memory, latency, privacy). KD methods operate at multiple granularities — softened output logits, intermediate feature or attention matching, relational and module-level objectives — and are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design, or data synthesis). Empirically, KD routinely improves student performance compared to training from scratch and enables deployment across modalities and constrained settings, though challenges remain in robustness, low-frequency behavior, domain shift, and distillation without original data. This synthesis summarizes core methods, practical workflows, empirical benefits, and open problems to guide applied KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses larger ‘‘teacher’’ models into smaller ‘‘student’’ models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations so students retain much of the teacher’s performance while reducing storage and inference cost. Distillation spans simple soft-target (logit) matching to richer forms that align intermediate features, attention maps, or decision-boundary information; practical deployments combine distillation with architecture-aware choices, selective data strategies, and complementary compression methods. The method is effective across vision and language tasks but has limits stemming from imperfect teachers, capacity mismatch, and data or distributional heterogeneity; careful method design and evaluation are required to realize robust, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Versatile Knowledge Distillation: Compression, Adaptation, and Robustness in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible paradigm for transferring information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient ones. Beyond simple logit matching, distillation techniques can be adapted to operate without original training data, guide architecture search, improve generalization under limited data, support cross-modal and multi-task transfer, and preserve or even enhance downstream performance on specialized tasks. When combined with task-aware search, feature-level imitation, and data augmentation strategies, distillation enables deployment of compact models that remain competitive with their teachers while meeting real-world constraints such as privacy, compute, and latency.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, empirically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. It supports multiple transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps), operates with or without original training data, and composes naturally with complementary methods (pre-training of compact models, pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much teacher performance, but it is not a panacea: practitioners must address capacity mismatch, data or distributional heterogeneity, and the risk of transferring undesirable behaviors (biases or adversarial vulnerabilities). A pragmatic deployment pipeline treats KD as one component in a compression strategy, matched to task constraints and combined with targeted mitigations for fairness, robustness, and heterogeneous-data scenarios.
